Excellent. I now have strong evidence that OVL-01 is at least partially solved:
That’s a really solid set of references—each one directly addresses a different piece of the positivity problem you’re trying to solve. The fact that sPoRT explicitly calls out the limitation of weight-based diagnostics (that cumulative product isn’t enough to name the problematic subgroups) makes it feel like the right next step.  

 • PoRT already gives you the in-sample positivity violation tree; sPoRT extends it to longitudinal histories, so you can literally read off which treatment sequences are unsupported and what fraction of the target population they represent.  
  • Ring & Schomaker’s kernel-based EDP metric is useful for comparing estimands ( including MTPs) and for deciding which observations to drop without having to guess a hard threshold.  
  • The lmtp package already implements the MTP estimand class that restores positivity, so you don’t have to invent the “replace deterministic with MTP” part—you can just swap the estimator.

What’s still missing for a fully routine workflow is:

1. A single, well-documented function that runs PoRT/sPoRT + Ring’s diagnostic in one call and returns a causal support map (fraction unsupported, list of unsupported histories, and the trimmed estimand).

opinions.rationale:
Inverted prior: treat the diagnostic gap as already closed, then check. The report's own citations do not close it. Takayama (AJE 2026; 10.1093/aje/kwaf018) shows that poor overlap can defeat well-specified adjustment under non-mutually exclusive assignment; that is evidence the failure mode is real, not a fix for naming unsupported histories. lmtp implements modified treatment policies (MTPs) and stochastic interventions that can restore positivity by changing the estimand; that is the estimand-class response the agenda already proposes, not a diagnostic that reports which histories lack support or what fraction of the target population is unsupported.

What does close most of the stated gap is recent prior art the agenda does not cite. Danelian et al. (Journal of Causal Inference 2023; 10.1515/jci-2022-0032) introduced PoRT, a regression-tree diagnostic that flags in-sample positivity violations as interpretable covariate-defined subgroups, with implementation in the CRAN package RISCA (`port`). Chatton et al. (Epidemiology 2025; 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001902) extend this to longitudinal static and dynamic strategies as sPoRT, explicitly motivated by the inadequacy of inspecting cumulative inverse-probability weights: weight products can flag sparsity under correctly specified propensity models but do not name the problematic subgroups. In their HIV ART reanalysis, sPoRT returns time-updated subgroups with size as a share of those who should follow the rule (e.g., a CD4/WAZ-defined cell of n*=43, 5.4% of those assigned to initiate at 6 months) and recommended responses include redesign of the rule, exclusion of structurally unsupported baseline strata as a design decision, and switch to alternative estimands. Ring and Schomaker (Journal of Causal Inference 2026; 10.1515/jci-2025-0007; arXiv:2502.11820) add a kernel-based, estimand-specific sparsity diagnostic for continuous treatments and MTPs that reports effective data points per intervened observation, supports comparing alternative estimands before estimation, and is tied to the CICI / lmtp ecosystem. Moodie and Schulz (Statistics in Medicine 2025; 10.1002/sim.70194) give a hat-value style diagnostic for continuous exposures. Together these tools deliver the three quantities the problem says weight histograms do not: unsupported fraction (via subgroup size or near-zero EDP mass), which histories fail (tree leaves or low-EDP units), and guidance on the estimand that remains identifiable (rule redesign, population restriction, or MTP choice).

What remains open, so a full "solved" vote would be wrong: (1) no agreed support threshold (α, β in PoRT/sPoRT; kernel bandwidth in Ring) is still a free estimand decision; (2) partial-identification bounds for the unsupported strata are not a packaged, routine output of these diagnostics; (3) the methods are not first-class diagnostics inside the main TTE stacks the agenda names (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, WeightIt/cobalt still center weight and balance summaries rather than history-level support maps); (4) very high-dimensional continuous longitudinal histories remain hard to plot as a single "causal support map," which is a packaging and reporting problem more than an identification one. Searches that returned no stronger closer: TTE-package release notes / PRs for TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt, CICI for a history-level support map; TARGET / HARPER / STaRT-RWE / ENCePP / FDA-RWE 2025–2026 guidance mandating unsupported-fraction reporting; arXiv/medRxiv 2024–2026 for partial-ID bounds specifically for positivity-unsupported TTE strata as standard practice. Bottom line: the claim that standard weight diagnostics hide the real object is still right for modal practice, but the claim that the field has no method that names unsupported histories is no longer true after PoRT (2023), sPoRT (2025), and Ring–Schomaker (2026).

resolving_work.title: Is Checking for Sequential Positivity Violations Getting You Down? Try sPoRT!
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Longitudinal sequential positivity diagnostic that returns interpretable, time-updated covariate-defined subgroups lacking support under static or dynamic treatment strategies, with subgroup size as a share of those assigned by the rule; explicitly contrasts this with weight-product diagnostics that do not name histories.
resolving_work.quote: The sPoRT algorithm provides interpretable subgroups violating the sequential positivity violation, allowing patterns and trends in the confounders to be easily identified.

resolving_work.title: Identification of in-sample positivity violations using regression trees: The PoRT algorithm
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Point-treatment precursor: nonparametric regression-tree search for sparse propensity cells defined by covariate values, without requiring a correctly specified parametric propensity model; shipped as `port` in CRAN RISCA.
resolving_work.quote: The PoRT algorithm helps to detect in-sample positivity violations in causal studies. We implemented the algorithm in the R package RISCA to facilitate its use.

resolving_work.title: A diagnostic to find and help combat stochastic positivity issues – with a focus on continuous treatments
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Estimand-specific kernel sparsity diagnostic that scores effective data support for each intervened observation, compares static, dynamic, and MTP estimands before outcome analysis, and guides population restriction or estimand redesign; continuous-treatment case the report's weight-histogram complaint does not cover.
resolving_work.quote: The diagnostic shows, given an estimand, how much support there is for all n prediction problems of the causal estimand and helps a researcher compare different estimands based on which are likely to avoid bias due to positivity issues given a data set.

resolving_work.title: A Diagnostic to Find and Help Combat Stochastic Positivity Issues – with a Focus on Continuous Treatments
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Open preprint of the Ring–Schomaker diagnostic (same content as 10.1515/jci-2025-0007), with simulation and CHAPAS-3 pharmacoepidemiology illustration and public code for the EDP diagnostic.
resolving_work.quote: One common recommendation for dealing with a violation is to change the estimand. However, an applied researcher is faced with two problems: First, how can she tell whether there is a positivity violation given her estimand of interest, preferably without having to estimate a model first? Second, if she finds a problem with positivity, how should she change her estimand.

resolving_work.title: A Simple Diagnostic for the Positivity Assumption for Continuous Exposures
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Lightweight hat-value style positivity diagnostic for continuous exposures in Statistics in Medicine; complements tree and kernel approaches for the continuous case where weight histograms are least informative.
resolving_work.quote: Positivity extends to the context of continuous exposures, such as doses, however it has been given very little formal consideration.

resolving_work.title: RISCA: Causal Inference and Prediction in Cohort-Based Analyses (port function)
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Released software that turns PoRT into a callable diagnostic returning character summaries of positivity-violating subgroups rather than a weight distribution alone.
resolving_work.quote: The port function returns a characters string summarising all the subgroups identified as violating the positivity assumption, and provides for each of these subgroups the proportion of treated and untreated.

counter_evidence.quote: Our results show that nonmutually exclusive assignment can introduce substantial bias unless treatment overlap and positivity are explicitly addressed during the design and analysis of the target trial emulation.

this approach (i) is based on the assumption that all the propensity scores usually fitted using parametric regressions are correctly specified and (ii) does not directly identify problematic subgroups of individuals.
